204.title: Vayeshev: God went down too (Genesis 39:2–3)
204.hook: even as a slave, "the LORD was with Joseph"
204.howItsDone: The teaching that the Shechinah, God's presence, went with Israel into every exile is a cornerstone of Jewish comfort, taught from the Talmud and echoed in prayer and song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a dry pit, and brothers sitting down to eat. Your line was no water in it. Did you reach someone at the bottom of something? Today, Joseph goes further down. Day two hundred four.

Picture the worst job you ever had. The night shift, the rude boss, the uniform that didn't fit, the sense that this was not where your life was supposed to be. Now make it worse. Joseph was pulled out of the pit and sold to a caravan of traders headed south. Seventeen, the favorite son, and now he's cargo. The Torah says Joseph was brought down to Egypt, and sold as a slave to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. Down, and down, and down. Today: God went down too.
screen: `THE WORST JOB YOU EVER HAD.` → `SOLD TO A CARAVAN.` → `BROUGHT DOWN TO EGYPT.`

segments.voice: You might expect the next line to be about despair. Instead, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man." In the house of his Egyptian master. Not after he was rescued. Not once things got better. There, as a slave. The Hebrew for prosperous is matzliach, someone whose work succeeds. And the next verse says his master saw it. He saw that God was with Joseph, and that whatever Joseph did, turned out well. So Potiphar puts him in charge of the whole house, and the Torah says the house of the Egyptian was blessed, for Joseph's sake. Notice what Joseph does in the lowest place. He works. He works well enough that a stranger notices something more than skill. He doesn't wait to be free before he's faithful. Now listen to a promise that comes later in Genesis. When the old Jacob is afraid to go down to Egypt himself, God tells him: "I will go down with thee into Egypt" and I'll bring you up again. God goes down too. The rabbis built a whole teaching on this. The Talmud says that wherever Israel went into exile, the Shechinah, God's presence, went with them. Into Egypt, into Babylon, into every hard place. It's one of the most comforting ideas in Jewish thought: the lowest place is not a place God has left. It doesn't make the pit less dark, or slavery less wrong. But Joseph, in a foreign house, with no family and no freedom, isn't alone.
screen: `THE LORD WAS WITH JOSEPH.` · `MATZLIACH: HIS WORK SUCCEEDS.` · `THE HOUSE BLESSED FOR HIS SAKE.` · `THE SHECHINAH GOES INTO EXILE.` · then, large: `GOD GOES DOWN WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do good work where you are. Settle, and breathe. Think about where you are right now, maybe not where you want to be. A job, a town, a stage of life. Pick one piece of work in front of you this week, however small. The dishes, a report, a shift. Picture doing it with care, the way Joseph did in a house that wasn't his. If you believe it, remember that God can be in that place too. The bell holds the time.
Vayeshev. And he settled: the portion where Joseph, sold as a slave in Egypt, does good work, and the LORD was with him there.
Your line: God goes down with you. Today, in one place you'd rather not be, do one piece of work as well as you can. Day two hundred four.

205.title: Vayeshev: why so sad today? (Genesis 40:6–7)
205.hook: in prison, Joseph notices two sad faces and asks why
205.tomorrow: at the end of two years
205.howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts receiving others with a pleasant face and noticing their distress as part of kindness, and Joseph's question in prison is taught as an example of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph a slave in Egypt, and the LORD was with him. Your line was God goes down with you. What work did you do well, in a place you'd rather not be? Day two hundred five.

When did someone last ask how you were, and wait for the real answer? The coworker who always says fine, the friend who laughs a little too fast, the kid who goes straight to their room: they're easy to walk past. There are problems enough of our own. Joseph has more than his share. Potiphar's wife accused him of something he refused to do, and he's been thrown into prison. Now he's the one looking after the other prisoners, including two of Pharaoh's officials: the chief cupbearer and the chief baker. One morning, he walks in. Today: why so sad today?
screen: `THE ONE WHO ALWAYS SAYS FINE.` → `FALSELY ACCUSED, IN PRISON.` → `ONE MORNING, HE WALKS IN.`

segments.voice: The two officials have each had a dream in the same night. In the morning, the Torah says, Joseph came in, looked at them, and saw that they were troubled. The Hebrew word, zo'afim, means upset, stormy, out of sorts. And Joseph asks them: why do your faces look so sad today? Stop there. Joseph is a prisoner himself. Sold by his brothers, falsely accused, far from home. He has every reason to be wrapped up in his own misery. Instead he notices two faces. Some readers love the word today in his question. Why so sad today? It means he knew what their faces usually looked like. He'd been paying attention all along, so he could see when something changed. They tell him: we dreamed, and there's nobody to interpret it. And Joseph answers, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" Tell me, please. The cupbearer tells his dream: a vine, three branches, grapes pressed into Pharaoh's cup. Joseph says: in three days you'll be restored. The baker's dream goes the other way. And all of it happens as Joseph said. This is the hinge of Joseph's whole life. Two years later, that cupbearer will remember a young Hebrew in prison who read dreams, and Joseph will stand before Pharaoh. His rise from the prison to the palace doesn't start with a miracle, or a clever plan. It starts with a question. A prisoner looks at two other prisoners and asks, what's wrong?

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask someone how they really are. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the faces you saw yesterday. A family member at breakfast, a coworker, a cashier, a neighbor. Did anyone look different than usual? More tired, quieter, stormier? Pick one of them. Picture yourself asking, gently, you seem a little off today, how are you really? And then just listening. The bell holds the time.
Vayeshev. And he settled: the portion that ends with Joseph in prison, noticing two sad faces and asking why.
Your line: notice the sad face. Today, look closely at one face you see every day, and if it looks different, ask how they really are. Day two hundred five.

screen: `DAY 205 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AT THE END OF TWO YEARS.`

206.title: Miketz: at the end of two years (Genesis 41:1, 14)
206.hook: the waiting ends in a day; Joseph is shaved and brought out
206.howItsDone: Miketz is read in synagogues in early winter, and Jews repeat the saying that God's help comes in the blink of an eye, yeshuat Hashem k'heref ayin, in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prisoner who noticed two sad faces. Your line was notice the sad face. Did you ask someone how they really were? Today, a new portion. Day two hundred six.

Waiting for the call back after the interview. Waiting for the test results. Waiting for the visa, the transplant list, the baby. Days that feel exactly like the day before. When Joseph read the cupbearer's dream, he asked him one thing: when you're free, remember me, and mention me to Pharaoh. The cupbearer was freed three days later. And the Torah says, with brutal simplicity, that he did not remember Joseph. He forgot him. The days go on in the dungeon. This portion is called Miketz, at the end. Today: at the end of two years.
screen: `WAITING FOR THE CALL.` → `REMEMBER ME.` → `HE FORGOT HIM.`

segments.voice: The portion opens, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And it came to pass at the end of two full years, that Pharaoh dreamed." Two full years. Morning after morning in a prison, after hope had come so close. The rabbis asked why two years. An old midrash, which Rashi brings, gives a hard answer: Joseph put his trust in the cupbearer, asking him twice to remember him, and so he waited two more years. Other teachers push back, gently: asking for help isn't wrong. The Torah itself doesn't say why. It only counts the time. And then, everything changes in a single day. Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, and nobody in Egypt can explain it. The cupbearer suddenly remembers. Oh. I have to confess something today. There was a young Hebrew in prison. Pharaoh sends for Joseph, and look how fast the verbs move: "they brought him hastily out of the dungeon." He shaves. He changes his clothes. He walks in before Pharaoh. From the dungeon to the king, with nothing in between but a razor and clean clothes. There's a Jewish saying: God's help comes in the blink of an eye. It isn't a promise about when. Joseph waited two full years, and nobody told him the date. But it's a reminder that long waiting and sudden change live side by side. The same prisoner who was forgotten is the one they're running to fetch. Miketz: at the end. Here, the end came all at once.
screen: `AT THE END OF TWO FULL YEARS.` · `WHY TWO YEARS?` · `BROUGHT HASTILY OUT OF THE DUNGEON.` · `HELP IN THE BLINK OF AN EYE.` · then, large: `IT ENDS SUDDENLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay ready for a sudden change. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been waiting on for a long time. Feel the weight of the waiting, honestly. Then picture Joseph, the morning they came running: he shaved, he changed his clothes, he was ready. What would being ready look like for you? One small thing you could keep in order, so that if the door opens, you can walk through. The bell holds the time.
Miketz. At the end: the portion that opens after two full years of waiting, and brings Joseph out of the dungeon in a single day.
Your line: it ends suddenly. Today, while you wait on something, do one thing to be ready for the day it changes. Day two hundred six.

screen: `DAY 206 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IT IS NOT IN ME.`

207.title: Miketz: it is not in me (Genesis 41:16)
207.hook: Joseph tells Pharaoh the meaning comes from God, not from him
207.howItsDone: Jewish learning takes care to cite who said what, and students repeat teachings in the name of the teacher who first taught them, following the Mishnah's saying about bringing redemption.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miketz: two full years of waiting, then out of the dungeon in a day. Your line was it ends suddenly. What did you do to be ready? Today, Joseph stands before Pharaoh. Day two hundred seven.

You finally get the meeting with the big boss. Or the audition. Or the chance to pitch the idea to the person who can make it happen. And they say: I hear you're the one who can do this. The easy reply is: yes, that's me. Joseph has just been pulled out of the dungeon, shaved and changed. He's standing in Pharaoh's court, a prisoner one hour ago. Pharaoh says: I've had a dream, and I've heard that you can read dreams. Today: it is not in me.
screen: `THE BIG MEETING.` → `I HEAR YOU'RE THE ONE.` → `A PRISONER BEFORE PHARAOH.`

segments.voice: Joseph's first words to Pharaoh, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace." In Hebrew, the first part is a single word, biladai. Not me. Apart from me. Think about the risk of saying that. Joseph needs Pharaoh to think he's valuable. He has one shot to get out of prison for good. And the first thing he does is hand the credit away. Remember the young Joseph, seventeen, telling his brothers about his dreams, where their sheaves bowed down to his? That Joseph talked a lot about himself. This one, after the pit and the prison, talks about God. And he keeps doing it. Pharaoh tells both dreams, the cows and the ears of grain, and Joseph says: God has told Pharaoh what he is about to do. Seven years of plenty, seven years of famine. The dream came twice because the thing is fixed by God, and God will do it soon. Again and again, in front of Pharaoh, Joseph names God. And here's the surprise. Giving the credit away doesn't make him smaller. Pharaoh looks around his court and asks: could we find anyone like this, a man with the spirit of God in him? And he puts Joseph over all of Egypt. The rabbis prized this. The Mishnah says that whoever repeats a teaching in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world. The lesson the rabbis drew from it is plain: say where things came from.
screen: `BILADAI: NOT ME.` · `THE BOY WHO TALKED ABOUT HIMSELF.` · `GOD HAS TOLD PHARAOH.` · `SAY IT IN THE NAME OF WHO SAID IT.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT IN ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give credit away once. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're proud of lately. A good result at work, a meal, a kid who's doing well, a hard day you got through. Now trace it back. Who taught you? Who helped? What was given to you that you didn't make yourself? If you pray, you can thank God for it. Either way, choose one person you could name out loud. The bell holds the time.
Miketz. At the end: the portion where Joseph, before Pharaoh, says the meaning isn't in him, but comes from God.
Your line: not in me. Today, when someone praises you for something, name one person, or one gift, that made it possible. Day two hundred seven.

208.title: Miketz: the Hanukkah portion
208.hook: Miketz almost always falls during Hanukkah: dreams and lights in the dark season
208.howItsDone: Jews light the Hanukkah menorah for eight nights, adding one light each night, often in a window, with blessings; on the Shabbat of Hanukkah, synagogues read Miketz and the prophetic reading from Zechariah's vision of the lampstand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, biladai: Joseph telling Pharaoh the answer wasn't in him. Your line was not in me. Who did you give credit to? Today, a portion and a holiday that keep meeting. Day two hundred eight.

Early winter, north of the equator. Dark by five. Cold car in the morning, dark driveway at night. And in window after window, small flames in a row, one more every night. That's Hanukkah. Hanukkah has fixed dates on the Jewish calendar, and the weekly Torah reading moves through the year in order, so the two keep meeting. The Shabbat of Hanukkah almost always reads Miketz, the portion of Pharaoh's dreams and Joseph's rise. Today: the Hanukkah portion.
screen: `DARK BY FIVE.` → `FLAMES IN THE WINDOWS.` → `MIKETZ MEETS HANUKKAH.`

segments.voice: First, the holiday. Hanukkah means dedication. In the time the books of the Maccabees describe, a Greek-Syrian king banned Jewish practice and set up an idol in the Temple in Jerusalem. A small band led by the Maccabee family rebelled, won, and rededicated the Temple. The Talmud adds the story of the oil: they found only one small jar of pure oil, enough for one day, and it burned for eight. So Jews light for eight nights, adding one light each night, as the school of Hillel taught, and set the lights where people outside can see them. Now, the portion. Miketz is full of dreams. Pharaoh's cows and grain. Joseph, who once dreamed as a boy, now reading dreams for a king. Seven fat years, seven lean, and a plan to get through the dark ones. Some readers hear a match between them: both are about light in a dark time. Hanukkah begins near the end of a Hebrew month, when the moon is thin, close to the longest nights of the year in the northern half of the world. And Joseph's story is a light in the dark, too: the prisoner forgotten for two years who ends up feeding the hungry from Egypt's stores. On the Shabbat of Hanukkah, the reading from the prophets is from Zechariah, who sees a golden lampstand in a vision. And in it, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit, saith the LORD of hosts." Dreams in the dark, lights in the dark. Neither one pretends the night is short. Each puts one small light in it.
screen: `HANUKKAH: DEDICATION.` · `ONE JAR OF OIL, EIGHT NIGHTS.` · `DREAMS AND A PLAN FOR LEAN YEARS.` · `NOT BY MIGHT, NOR BY POWER.` · then, large: `DREAMS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle and recall a dream. If you have a candle and it's safe, light it now. If not, picture one, a single small flame. Settle, and breathe. Watch the light. Then remember a dream you once had for your life. Not a night dream, a hope. Maybe one that got put away in a dark year. Hold it near the flame for a while. You don't have to decide anything. Just let it be seen. The bell holds the time.
Miketz. At the end: the portion of Pharaoh's dreams, almost always read on the Shabbat of Hanukkah, with lights in the dark.
Your line: dreams in the dark. Tonight, when it gets dark, turn on one light on purpose, and let it remind you of one hope you haven't given up. Day two hundred eight.

209.title: Miketz: guilt remembers (Genesis 42:21)
209.hook: years later the brothers say "We are verily guilty concerning our brother"
209.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur, Jews confess together in the plural, beginning ashamnu, we have been guilty, and Jewish teaching on teshuvah includes naming the wrong aloud and seeking to repair it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hanukkah portion: Pharaoh's dreams and lights in the dark season. Your line was dreams in the dark. What light did you turn on? Today, the famine reaches Canaan. Day two hundred nine.

Something you did at fourteen. A cruel thing you said to a kid at school. You haven't thought about it in years. Then one day, something small, a song, a name, a face in a crowd, and it's right there again, as sharp as the day it happened. Famine has come, just as Joseph said. In Canaan, Jacob sends ten of his sons down to Egypt to buy grain. They stand before the governor of Egypt, and bow low. They don't recognize him. He recognizes them. Today: guilt remembers.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU DID AT FOURTEEN.` → `TEN BROTHERS, BOWING.` → `THEY DON'T RECOGNIZE HIM.`

segments.voice: Joseph speaks to them harshly, through an interpreter. You're spies. You've come to find the weak spots in our land. They protest: we're honest men, twelve brothers, sons of one father. The youngest is at home with our father, and one is no more. Joseph puts them in custody for three days. Then he tells them: one of you stays in prison, the rest take grain home, and bring me your youngest brother. And right there, in front of him, the brothers start talking to each other in Hebrew, thinking the Egyptian can't understand. And what comes out, more than twenty years after the pit, is this, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother." We saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. That's why this distress has come on us. Notice what they remember. Not just the act. His begging. The Torah never told us, back at the pit, that Joseph pleaded with them. We only learn it now, from their memory. Guilt kept a detail that the story itself left out. Reuben adds: didn't I tell you not to sin against the boy? And you wouldn't listen. And Joseph, who understands every word, turns away from them and weeps. The Hebrew phrase the brothers use, aval ashemim anachnu, is where their teshuvah, their turning back, begins. Its key word is ashem, guilty, which echoes in the confession Jews say on Yom Kippur: ashamnu, we have been guilty. Said together, out loud. Guilt remembers. And remembering is where repair begins.
screen: `YOU ARE SPIES.` · `ONE OF US IS NO MORE.` · `WE SAW HIS DISTRESS, AND WOULD NOT HEAR.` · `JOSEPH TURNS AWAY AND WEEPS.` · then, large: `WE ARE VERILY GUILTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name a guilt you still carry. Settle, and breathe. Let one old thing come up, something you did, or didn't do, that still stings. Don't argue with it, and don't drown in it. Just name it, quietly, the way the brothers did: I did this. I saw, and didn't listen. If you pray, you can bring it to God. Then ask: is there anything, even small, I could do to repair it? The bell holds the time.
Miketz. At the end: the portion where, years later, the brothers finally say out loud, we are verily guilty concerning our brother.
Your line: guilt remembers. Today, if an old wrong comes to mind, don't push it away. Write it down, or take one small step toward making it right. Day two hundred nine.

210.title: Miketz: weeping in private (Genesis 43:30–31)
210.hook: Joseph leaves to cry, washes his face, and comes back in
210.howItsDone: Jewish tradition makes room for tears in prayer, especially on the High Holy Days, and teaches that the gates of tears are not locked; Joseph's weeping is read each winter in Miketz and Vayigash.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brothers saying out loud, we are verily guilty. Your line was guilt remembers. This week: God going down into Egypt, a sad face noticed, two years ending in a day, not in me, dreams in the dark, and guilt. Today, Joseph's tears. Day two hundred ten.

You're at work, or at a wedding, or a kid's recital, and something hits you. A memory, a face, a piece of news. Your throat closes. And you say, excuse me, one second, and walk fast down the hallway to the bathroom, and lock the door. The brothers have come back to Egypt, and this time they've brought the youngest, Benjamin. Joseph's only full brother, the other son of Rachel. The last time Joseph saw him, Benjamin was just a boy. Today: weeping in private.
screen: `EXCUSE ME, ONE SECOND.` → `BENJAMIN COMES TO EGYPT.` → `THE OTHER SON OF RACHEL.`

segments.voice: Joseph asks them about their father: is the old man well? Is he still alive? Then he lifts his eyes and sees Benjamin, his mother's son. Is this your youngest brother, the one you told me about? And he says to him: God be gracious to you, my son. And then, the Torah says, Joseph hurried. His compassion for his brother welled up, the Hebrew says, it grew warm inside him, and he looked for a place to cry. "And he entered into his chamber, and wept there." Then, three short actions. "And he washed his face." He came out. And he held himself back, the Hebrew word is vayit'apak, he restrained himself, and said: serve the meal. Stop and look at that sequence. He doesn't pretend nothing happened. He lets himself cry, fully, alone. And then he washes his face and walks back into the room, because the room still needs him. There's a plan in motion, and a family that isn't ready to know who he is yet. Joseph cries again and again in Genesis: when the brothers confess, here, when he finally reveals himself, when he falls on Benjamin's neck, when he sees his father, when his father dies, and when his brothers ask forgiveness. The man who runs Egypt for Pharaoh is a man who weeps. The Talmud does not treat tears as weakness. It says that since the Temple was destroyed, the gates of prayer have been locked, but the gates of tears have not. But there's also a time to wash your face. Both are part of it.
